view.text:
11:47 PM. The storm has been working at the windows for an hour.

Someone knocks. Three times, evenly, the way people knock when they already know you're home.

Through the peephole: a woman in a dark coat, soaked through, hair flat against her face. She isn't shivering. She is looking straight into the lens, as if she can see you on the other side of it.

"Please," she says. "You already let me in."

You have never seen her before. Your hand is on the deadbolt. In your pocket, your thumb finds the bus ticket.

You turn the deadbolt. It is loud in the narrow entry, louder than it should be.

On the other side of the door, nothing. No knock. No footsteps. Then, softly, almost kindly:

"That's all right. You did, though."

Water runs out from under the door in a thin, straight line, as if it has somewhere to be.

She crosses the hall to 6D and knocks. Teo's door. Teo, who has lived across from you for six years and has never once opened his door to anyone. Not the super, not the police that night in March, not you.

She waits. He doesn't open. She says something to the wood that you can't hear.

Then she walks to the stairwell, and the fire door sighs shut behind her. Down. Not up. You can hear her going down for a long time.

The lights go out at 11:58. The fridge stops humming, and in the quiet you hear the building the way you never do: pipes, wind in the elevator shaft, something settling in the walls.

You sit on the floor with your back against the locked door, because it seems like the only fixed thing in the apartment.

Somewhere far below, a metal door closes. Then, very faintly, someone laughs.

It sounds like you.

view.text:
At 12:06 there is a sound at Teo's door: the chain, the bolt, the chain again. It opens two inches. One eye. A strip of grey cardigan.

"She was in there," he says. "With you. I heard her in your apartment."

You start to tell him that's impossible, that your door has been locked all night.

"I know," he says. "I heard you lock it. I heard both." He looks toward the stairwell. "She went down. If you go after her, don't go down. Go up. Up is just weather."

The door closes. The chain.

Six flights in the dark, one hand on the rail. The basement is dry, which is wrong; the storm is everywhere else.

Storage cages in rows, numbered in stencil. At the far end, unit 07, still padlocked. Mara sits on the concrete in front of it with the brass key in her lap, as if she is waiting for a bus.

"There you are," she says. "Both of you are late."

"A night," she says. "Not this one. One somebody put away instead of living it."

She stands and steps aside. The cage door is held by a padlock you have never seen on anything in this building: no keyhole, just four brass dials, green at the edges.

"The key was never for that," Mara says. "I never had the number."

She looks at your pocket.

"You do."

The dials are cold and stiff. 1146.

The shackle drops open with a sound like a held breath let go.

Inside 07 there is a folding chair, facing the door. On the seat lies a bus ticket. Yours: the same crease, the same small stain. But old, and dry, as if it has been waiting here for years. Whatever was written on it has faded almost to nothing.

Mara doesn't go in. "That's what's in 07," she says. "Every time."

view.text:
The night comes apart in your hands, and for a moment you can see all of it: the night you lived, and the nights you didn't.

Everything that crossed over came from somewhere. Touch a thread to see where.

choices: Open the door and let it through
view.text:
Somewhere below you, or behind you, or inside the walls, a door is waiting to be opened. You know which one. It is the one you didn't choose.

You can close it for good. Or you can open it and let the other night through.

You open the door.

The other night comes in quietly, the way Mara did. It smells like rain that never reached this building.

The two nights no longer agree about the brass key. Here, it is in Mara's hand, beside you. In the other night, it is with Mara, in the stairwell. Your bus ticket is in your hand, in both nights.

The worlds no longer agree on where Mara is. Here, she is beside you. In the other night, she is in the stairwell.

In 6D, Teo turns off his radio, and you hear him say, to no one, "Finally."

You look at what the night left you. "1146" on the bus ticket, in Mara's handwriting. "ROOF" on the key's paper tag, in Mara's handwriting. Both written in a night you never lived.

Both nights are true now.
